definition: A simple, hymn-like melody, especially one associated with the German Protestant church, or a harmonised setting of such a tune.
origin: From German Choral (Choralgesang, choral song), from medieval Latin cantus choralis (song of the choir), from Latin chorus (a choir, a dance). Martin Luther championed congregational chorales in the 16th century so worshippers themselves could sing.

definition: An orchestral piece that introduces an opera, oratorio, or other large work, or a standalone concert piece in a similar style.
origin: From French ouverture (opening), from ouvrir (to open), from Latin aperire (to open). By the 17th century, composers wrote an instrumental overture to open the audience's ears before the curtain rose.
